strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: exploiting available slot annotations to improve dialogue utterance embeddings without intent-label supervision during encoder training. Template augmentation and utterance–template contrastive learning form a practical, understandable approach.

Experiments cover five intent-classification datasets. Table 3 reports average accuracy of 83.87 for TaDSE with MLP versus 81.82 for DSE, and includes baselines trained with the proposed augmented data.

The loss ablations provide useful evidence beyond augmentation alone. In Table 5, adding template and pairwise losses improves over utterance-only training on all three reported datasets. The discussion also acknowledges dataset-dependent augmentation quality and noisy entity extraction.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol needs clarification before the results support a clear Findings recommendation. Appendix B uses full utterance/template training-set representations for nearest-neighbor classification, but does not establish whether every baseline receives an identical reference pool, whether synthetic examples enter that pool, or how ambiguous templates receive intent labels. These choices can improve retrieval independently of encoder quality.

The supervision framing overstates what is demonstrated. Four datasets supply annotated slots, and classification uses labeled training references. The encoder is trained without intent labels, but the overall pipeline is not annotation-free. The source of test-time templates for semantic compression—gold slots or predicted slots—is also unspecified, materially affecting practical applicability.

The semantic-compression analysis has a concrete unresolved measurement issue. Figure 8 reports uniformity values around -12, outside the [-8, 0] range permitted by Equation 6 for unit-normalized embeddings. Normalization and the metric implementation must be clarified. Moreover, interpolation toward a shared template mechanically contracts within-template distances before renormalization, so improved alignment alone does not validate the proposed interpretation of the compression coefficient as semantic quality.

The contrastive objective does not fully account for the proposed many-to-one relationship. In Equation 3, another utterance sharing the anchor's template becomes a negative if it occurs in the same batch. Comparing distinct utterances does not guarantee incorrect template–utterance pairings. The paper should specify duplicate handling or template-aware sampling and assess this conflict.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful configuration appendix. Contrastive temperatures, optimizer settings, precise baseline adaptation procedures, and MLP integration are insufficiently specified. In particular, Equation 3 uses untransformed templates while inference uses transformed templates, leaving the claimed alignment mechanism unclear. Code is only promised.

The claimed significance and stability are not supported by repeated-run variability or statistical tests. Some compression gains are only 0.29–0.57 percentage points on SNIPS, corresponding to roughly two to four test examples. Appendix C also motivates different training durations using test-set learning curves; an explicit validation-only epoch-selection protocol is needed.

The broader claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Evaluation concerns English intent classification with full labeled reference sets, rather than few-shot annotation savings or general dialogue understanding. Relevant cited alternatives such as EASE and DiffCSE are absent from the comparisons, limiting the state-of-the-art claim. These scope limitations are separate from the evaluation and reproducibility issues driving the resubmission recommendation.
